newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: "Shark pack" S Africans sorry for killing American.
newsitem.headline: "Shark pack" S Africans sorry for killing American.

text.p: Four black South Africans who killed a white U.S. student four years ago apologised to her parents on Tuesday for what a lawyer described as an attack by sharks in a feeding frenzy.

The four, serving 18-year prison terms for the August 1993 murder of Amy Biehl in Gugulethu township outside Cape Town, issued the apologies during a public application for amnesty to Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

Biehl's parents, Peter and Linda, have flown to South Africa from California to attend the hearings. They have said they do not oppose the amnesty applications, part of South Africa's attempts to heal the wounds of the apartheid race war.

The four blacks -- Easy Mzikhona Nofemela, Vusumzi Ntamo, Ntobeko Peni and Mongezi Manqina -- said in statements to the commission that the killing was part of their larger aim to win South Africa back for the black majority.
A lawyer acting for the commission, Robin Brink, asked Nofemela if the murder was no more than "wanton brutality, carried out like a pack of sharks smelling blood".
Nofemela rejected the description. "She came to Guguletu at the very wrong moment. The students really wanted the land to be returned to Africans," he said.
Ntamo acknowledged in a statement to the commission that he was mentally backward and described himself as someone who followed others.
"I think I do suffer from some mental incapacity," he said. "I am not able to properly articulate any political ideology or motivation for my conduct."

In their statements the four, all now in their early 20s, described chasing Biehl across a street after her car was stopped by a crowd of youths who had attended a meeting of the radical Pan Africanist Congress (PAC).
Manqina told the commission he had tripped Biehl and delivered what he believed was the fatal knife wound while she lay on the ground. Other youths rained rocks on her body.
Peni said the crowd had been "in high spirits".
"We had no mercy on white people," he added.
He said he had realised later that Biehl was trying to help South Africa's blacks and he regretted having taken part in killing her.
"I realise it was bad," Peni said. "I ask Amy's parents to forgive me. Just to hear they have forgiven me would mean a great deal to me."
Biehl's parents, who are due to address the hearing later on Tuesday, shook hands at the start of proceedings with family and friends of the four youths.
The four said in their statements that they were influenced by the PAC slogan "one settler, one bullet", and understood this to mean that all whites should be killed.
"Killing every white person meant the land would come back to the African people," Peni said.

The Truth Commission was set up in 1995 to investigate human rights abuses by all sides during more than four decades of apartheid. It has powers to grant amnesty to perpetrators who make full confessions.

At the time Biehl was murdered, South Africa was in the final stages of preparing for all-race elections in April 1994 that marked the final end of apartheid. The PAC won less that two percent of the vote.
